CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should continue to retaliate in kind against U.S. tariffs, matching each escalation with proportional counter-tariffs on American agricultural and industrial goods, while signaling willingness to negotiate if the U.S. de-escalates. Retaliation preserves China's credibility and leverage, while avoiding actions that would escalate beyond the current tit-for-tat dynamic.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not yet existential. The U.S. has imposed 25% tariffs on $34 billion of Chinese goods (July 6, 2018) and has threatened up to $250 billion total, targeting machinery and high-tech items central to Made in China 2025 (RAND analysis). China's exports to the U.S. represent roughly 5% of GDP ($505 billion), making the trade war a material drag on export-dependent sectors. However, several factors mitigate the threat: (1) the yuan has already depreciated ~6% from 6.28 to 6.64 per dollar since April, partially offsetting tariff impacts (RAND); (2) China's retaliatory tariffs target U.S. agricultural products and consumer goods that are easily re-sourced from other countries like Brazil and Australia (RAND); (3) the Trump administration is motivated by midterm election politics and may seek a face-saving deal after November 2018 (Brookings/Dollar). China's retaliation is constrained by the trade asymmetry—China imports only $130 billion of U.S. goods versus $505 billion in exports—but China can adjust tariff rates higher to compensate (RAND). The CFR analysis shows China's industrial policy (technology transfer requirements, domestic subsidies, buy-China procurement) is the real U.S. target, and conceding on these structural issues would undermine China's long-term development strategy. Retaliation maintains negotiating leverage while protecting core interests.
key_factors: U.S. tariffs on $34B of Chinese goods at 25% effective July 6, 2018; threat of $250B+ total
Yuan depreciation of ~6% (6.28 to 6.64/USD) partially offsets tariff impact
China's exports to U.S. ~5% of GDP ($505B) vs U.S. exports to China ~0.7% of GDP ($130B) — asymmetric vulnerability
China's retaliation targets easily re-sourcable agricultural/consumer goods
U.S. midterm election timing suggests potential window for deal after November 2018
U.S. targeting of Made in China 2025 and technology transfer policies — core strategic interests at stake

sources_cited.excerpt: From early April, when the talk of trade wars began in earnest and the Chinese yuan was valued at 6.28 to the dollar, the currency has depreciated by 6 percent to 6.64 to the dollar as of July 6
$505 billion in potentially lost exports is a much larger slice of the Chinese economy (about 5 percent) than $130 billion is for the United States (about 0.7 percent)

For the next several months we will probably be locked into this situation. No high-level negotiations are scheduled. The Trump administration sees this as a winning strategy for the midterm elections in 2018.
China's industrial policy largely shifted from export promotion to import substitution after 2009
The Chinese have targeted lower-technology and consumer-facing goods. These are unlikely to disrupt producer supply chains. These items are also relatively easy to source from other countries.
